{{Short description|Cubic plane curve}}
[[File:Neil-parab-3.svg|thumb|Semicubical parabola for various {{mvar|a}}]]
In [[mathematics]], a '''cuspidal cubic''' or '''semicubical parabola''' is an [[algebraic plane curve]] that has an [[implicit equation]] of the form
<math display=">
 y^2 - a^2 x^3 = 0
</math>
(with {{math|''a'' ≠ 0}}) in some [[Cartesian coordinate system]].

Solving for {{mvar|y}} leads to the [[implicit equation|explicit  form]]
<math display="block">
 y = \pm a x^{\frac{3}{2}},
</math>
which implies that every [[real number|real]] point satisfies {{math|''x'' ≥ 0}}. The exponent explains the term ''semicubical parabola''. (A [[parabola]] can be described by the equation {{math|1=''y'' = ''ax''{{sup|2}}}}.)

Solving the implicit equation for {{mvar|x}} yields a second explicit form
<math display="block">
 x = \left(\frac{y}{a}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}.
</math>

The [[parametric equation]]
<math display="block">
 x = t^2, \quad y = a t^3
</math>
can also be deduced from the implicit equation by putting <math>t = \tfrac{y}{ax}.</math><ref name="pickover">{{citation |title=The Math Book: From Pythagoras to the 57th Dimension, 250 Milestones in the History of Mathematics |first=Clifford A. |last=Pickover |author-link=Clifford Pickover |publisher=Sterling Publishing Company, Inc. |year=2009 |isbn=9781402757969 |page=148 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JrslMKTgSZwC&pg=PA148 |contribution=The Length of Neile's Semicubical Parabola}}.</ref>

The semicubical parabolas have a [[Cusp (singularity)|cuspidal singularity]]; hence the name of ''cuspidal cubic''.

The arc length of the curve was calculated by the English mathematician [[William Neile]] and published in 1657 (see [[#History|section History]]).<ref>August Pein: ''Die semicubische oder Neil'sche Parabel, ihre Sekanten und Tangenten'' {{in lang|de}}, p.&nbsp;2.</ref>

== Properties of semicubical parabolas ==
=== Similarity ===
Any semicubical parabola <math>(t^2,at^3)</math> is '''[[Similarity (geometry)|similar]]''' to the ''semicubical unit parabola'' {{nowrap|<math>(u^2,u^3)</math>.}}

''Proof:'' The similarity <math> (x,y) \rightarrow (a^2x,a^2y) </math> (uniform scaling) maps the semicubical parabola <math>(t^2,at^3)</math> onto the curve <math>((at)^2,(at)^3) = (u^2,u^3)</math> with {{nowrap|<math>u=at </math>.}}

=== Singularity ===
The parametric representation <math>(t^2,at^3)</math> is ''[[Regular curve|regular]] except'' at point {{nowrap|<math>(0,0)</math>.}} At point <math>(0,0)</math> the curve has a ''[[Singularity (mathematics)|singularity]]'' (cusp). The ''proof'' follows from the tangent vector {{nowrap|<math> (2t,3t^2)</math>.}} Only for <math>t=0</math> this vector has zero length.
[[File:Neil-parab-t.svg|thumb|Tangent at a semicubical parabola]]

=== Tangents ===
Differentiating the ''semicubical unit parabola'' <math>y = \pm x^{3/2}</math> one gets at point <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> of the ''upper'' branch the equation of the tangent:
:<math> y = \frac{\sqrt{x_0}}{2}\left(3x-x_0\right)  .</math>
This tangent intersects the ''lower'' branch at exactly one further point with coordinates <ref>August Pein: ''Die semicubische oder Neil'sche Parabel, ihre Sekanten und Tangenten '', p.26</ref> 
:<math> \left(\frac{x_0}{4}, -\frac{y_0}{8}\right) .</math>
(Proving this statement one should use the fact, that the tangent meets the curve at <math>(x_0,y_0) </math> twice.)

=== Arclength ===
Determining the [[arclength]] of a curve <math>(x(t),y(t))</math> one has to solve the integral <math display="inline"> \int \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} \;dt .</math> For the semicubical parabola <math>(t^2,at^3), \; 0\le t\le b ,</math> one gets 
:<math> \int^b_0\sqrt{x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2} \;dt = \int^b_0 t\sqrt{4+9a^2t^2}\; dt = \cdots = \left[\frac{1}{27a^2} \left(4 + 9a^2t^2\right)^\frac{3}{2}\right]^b_0\; .</math>
(The integral can be solved by the [[Integration by substitution|substitution]] {{nowrap|<math>u=4+9a^2t^2</math>.)}}

''Example:'' For {{math|1=''a'' = 1}} (semicubical unit parabola) and {{math|1=''b'' = 2,}} which means the length of the arc between the origin and point (4,8), one gets the arc length 9.073.

=== Evolute of the unit parabola ===
The [[evolute#Evolute of a parabola|evolute of the ''parabola'']] <math> (t^2,t)</math> is a semicubical parabola shifted by 1/2 along the ''x''-axis: <math display="inline">\left(\frac{1}{2}+t^2,\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}^3}t^3\right).</math>

=== Polar coordinates ===
In order to get the representation of the semicubical parabola <math>(t^2,at^3)</math> in polar coordinates, one determines the intersection point of the line <math> y=mx</math> with the curve. For <math> m\ne 0</math> there is one point different from the origin: <math display="inline"> \left(\frac{m^2}{a^2}, \frac{m^3}{a^2}\right).</math> This point has distance <math display="inline">\frac{m^2}{a^2}\sqrt{1+m^2}</math> from the origin. With <math> m=\tan \varphi</math> and <math>\sec^2 \varphi = 1 + \tan^2\varphi </math> ( see [[List of trigonometric identities#Pythagorean identities|List of identities]]) one gets <ref>August Pein: ''Die semicubische oder Neil'sche Parabel, ihre Sekanten und Tangenten '', p. 10</ref>
:<math> r=\left(\frac{\tan\varphi}{ a}\right)^2 \sec \varphi \; ,\quad -\frac{\pi}{2} < \varphi < \frac{\pi}{2} . </math>

[[File:Neil-parab-p.svg|250px|thumb|Relation between a semicubical parabola and a ''cubic'' function (green)]]

=== Relation between a semicubical parabola and a cubic function ===
Mapping the semicubical parabola <math>(t^2,t^3)</math> by the [[projective map]] <math display="inline"> (x,y) \rightarrow \left(\frac{x}{y}, \frac{1}{y}\right)</math> ([[Involution (mathematics)|involutory]] [[Perspective (geometry)|perspectivity]] with axis <math> y=1</math> and center {{nowrap|<math>(0,-1)</math>)}} yields <math display="inline"> \left(\frac{1}{t}, \frac{1}{t^3}\right),</math> hence the ''cubic function'' <math>y=x^3.</math> The cusp (origin) of the semicubical parabola is exchanged with the [[point at infinity]] of the y-axis.

This property can be derived, too, if one represents the semicubical parabola by ''[[homogeneous coordinates]]'': In equation '''(A)''' the replacement <math> x=\tfrac{x_1}{x_3}, \; y=\tfrac{x_2}{x_3}</math> (the line at infinity has equation {{nowrap|<math>x_3=0</math>.)}} and the multiplication by <math> x_3^3</math> is performed. One gets the equation of the curve 
*in ''homogeneous coordinates'': <math> x_3 x_2^2 - x_1^3 = 0 .</math>
Choosing line <math> x_{\color{red}2}=0</math> as line at infinity and introducing <math> x=\tfrac{x_1}{x_2}, \; y=\tfrac{x_3}{x_2}</math> yields the (affine) curve <math> y=x^3.</math>

=== Isochrone curve ===
An additional defining property of the semicubical parabola is that it is an ''[[isochrone curve]]'', meaning that a particle following its path while being pulled down by gravity travels equal vertical intervals in equal time periods. In this way it is related to the ''tautochrone curve'', for which particles at different starting points always take equal time to reach the bottom, and the [[brachistochrone curve]], the curve that minimizes the time it takes for a falling particle to travel from its start to its end.

==History==
The semicubical parabola was discovered in 1657 by [[William Neile]] who computed its [[arc length]]. Although the lengths of some other non-algebraic curves including the [[logarithmic spiral]] and [[cycloid]] had already been computed (that is, those curves had been ''rectified''), the semicubical parabola was the first [[algebraic curve]] (excluding the [[Line (geometry)|line]] and [[circle]]) to be rectified.<ref name="pickover"/>{{disputed inline|for=It appears that [[parabola]] and other [[conic section]]s have been rectified a long time before|date=April 2015}}

The length of the semicubical parabola was computed by [[van Heuraet]] in 1659.<ref>[[V. J. Katz]] & F. Swetz, [https://web.archive.org/web/20240418002425/https://maa.org/press/periodicals/convergence/mathematical-treasures-van-heuraets-rectification-of-curves Van Heuraet's Rectifaction of Curves], ''Convergence'', via Wayback Machine</ref>
